Students Needing Extended Scaffolds
	Provide a copy of the Edit Checklist with visual examples of each editing skill.
Review one editing skill at a time:
• Capital letters
• Spaces between words
• End punctuation
Meet with students in a small group to model how to locate and correct errors in a draft.
Provide sentence examples showing:
Incorrect: water moves through rivers
Correct: Water moves through rivers.
Students may:
• Highlight errors before correcting them
• Verbally explain edits to a teacher or partner
• Participate in shared editing before independently editing their own draft
Sentence Frames:
• I fixed a _____ letter.
• I added a _____.
• I corrected _____.


	Students Approaching Independence
	Provide:
• Edit Checklist
• Peer editing opportunities
• Color-coded editing tools (highlighters, colored pencils)
Encourage students to edit one checklist item at a time.
Checklist:
□ I checked capital letters.
□ I checked spaces.
□ I checked punctuation.
□ I fixed mistakes I found.
Students discuss edits with a partner before making corrections independently.


	Students Who Are Independent
	Challenge students to:
• Explain why edits improve readability.
• Identify additional errors not listed on the checklist.
• Support peers during editing conferences.
• Review sentence fluency while editing.
• Prepare writing for publishing by ensuring all edits are complete. 
	ELL/Multilingual Learners
	Provide:
• Visual examples of correct and incorrect sentences
• Color-coded editing models
• Partner rehearsal before editing
• Teacher modeling and think-alouds
• Bilingual supports when available
Sentence Frames:
• I found a mistake in _____.
• I added a capital letter.
• I added punctuation.
Students may orally explain edits before making corrections in writing.


	Transcription Demands Addressed
	Students focus on editing conventions after ideas have already been developed during planning, drafting, and revising. The Edit Checklist breaks editing into manageable steps so students can focus on one skill at a time. Teacher modeling, oral rehearsal, peer support, color-coded editing tools, and visual examples reduce cognitive load while reinforcing capitalization, spacing, and punctuation conventions. Students are encouraged to reread their writing aloud to identify errors and improve overall readability before publishing.

□ I can use the Edit Checklist to review my writing.

	 Glows & Grows Written feedback/conference

PART 1: UNIT 1 COMMUNITY VOCABULARY BANK
Directions: Introduce and revisit these high-leverage words throughout the unit. Encourage second-grade students to use them actively during oral turn-and-talk discussions, visual analyses, and formal explanatory writing.
Vocabulary Word
	Student-Friendly Definition
	Instructional Strategy / Routine
	citizen
	A person who is a member of a community.
	Say It / Ask: How can you be a good citizen in your classroom community?
	community
	A group of people who live, work, or play together.
	Define It / Use It: Our neighborhood community includes people who live close to us.
	cooperate
	When you cooperate, you work with others to do something.
	Frame It: If we cooperate, we can _____.
	volunteer
	A person who helps others without getting paid.
	Use It / Ask: What have you done as a volunteer?
	 
PART 2: UNIT 1 SENTENCE FRAME BANK
Directions: Deploy these structured, scaffolded linguistic structures across the six-week unit cycle. They are optimized for oral peer interactions, reading comprehension, articulation, and formal explanatory composition phases.
Week 1 - Building Ideas & Topic Introduction
·        Think of a time when you helped someone in your community.
·        How did you know what they needed?
·        I helped a community member when _____.
·        I noticed that they needed support with _____.
Week 2 - Analyzing Visual and Informational Texts
·        I learned that community members can care for each other by _____.
·        Good citizens do their part to help by _____.
·        When you summarize, you put the most important ideas in a text into your own words.
Week 3 - Developing Topics & Text Evidence
·        In my opinion, an important way to serve our community is _____ because _____.
·        The author's purpose in Doing Your Part: Serving Your Community is to teach readers about _____.
·        One key detail from paragraph 30 that supports this purpose is _____.
Week 4 - Process Writing: Planning and Drafting
·        The primary reason citizens should cooperate is _____.
·        I am organizing my explanatory piece by first introducing the community topic and then providing facts from the text.
Week 5 - Process Writing: Revising and Editing
·        I used a simple sentence to clearly share information about _____.
·        I verified that my proper nouns begin with a capital letter, like the title of the text.
Week 6 - Publishing and Reflecting
·        This text successfully shows how community members help each other because _____.
·        I chose to share my final explanatory writing piece with our class community because _____.


 
PART 3: EXPLANATORY WRITING STUDENT CHECKLIST
Directions: Distribute this self-monitoring rubric to students during the drafting, revision, and editing phases (Module 1, Sessions 25–30). Instruct them to verify compliance before publishing.
☐   I stated a clear main idea about how community members care for each other.
☐   I provided two strong facts from paragraph 30 'Try It!' to support my answer.
☐   I used simple sentences to connect my thoughts clearly.
☐   I checked my spelling and made sure my words use correct short vowel and closed syllable patterns.
☐   I identified and used proper nouns correctly with capital letters.
☐   I used capital letters at the beginning of sentences and for specific names or titles.
☐   I used correct punctuation (. , ? !) at the end of every sentence.
☐   I left clear spaces between my words so it is easy for my audience to read.
☐   My writing makes complete sense when I read it out loud to myself or a partner.

Unit Procedure (Weekly Days Overview):
Each lesson spans four days, focusing on formation of letters. Each lesson is designed for approximately 10 -15 minutes of instruction.The final day is for review and assessment.
Day 1:Evaluate/Pretest  (15 mins.)
* Model: Write or display the  letters of the alphabet on the board or chart paper. As you point to the letters, invite students to sing the ABC song with you. Tell students that during handwriting they will be learning to write the letters of the alphabet and numbers appropriately. 
* Practice:

* Wrap Up/Recap: As students write, take notes of their handwriting skills and areas that you need to support. 
   * Use the Mastery Behaviors checklist to assess student progress. 
   * Keep this sample to compare student handwriting BOY, MOY, and EOY.
Day 2: Handwriting Paper  (10 mins.)
* Model:
   * Explain to students that when we write we have special lines on our writing paper that help us make our letters look neat and tidy.
   * Display for students sheet of lined handwriting paper (preferably chart paper or newsprint, with blue headline, dashed blue midline, and red endline). 
   * The Headline- this line is at the very top. Some of our letters are super tall and touch the headline. Ask students if they can think of a letter that goes all the way to the top (b,d, f, h, k, l, t). Model writing these letters.
   * The Midline- this line is in the middle and it is different- it’s a dashed line. Some of our letters are short and only go up to the midline. They’re short and do not peek over (a, c, e, i, m, n, o, r, s, u, v, w, x, z).  Model writing a few of these letters. 
   * The Red Endline- this line is at the bottom. This line is known as the “endline.” Some of our letters rest on the endline while there will be others that will go under the endline (a, c, e, - under the endline- j, g, y). 
* Guide:
   * Guide students through using handwriting paper to make the basic strokes. Some strokes should start at the headline or midline.
* Practice:
   * Have students practice tracing the basic strokes on the handwriting paper. 
* Wrap-up/Recap: What did we learn today? What are the names of each line on the paper. 
Day 3:  Review of  Writing Positions and Basic Strokes- Vertical Lines (10 mins.)
* Model:  
   * Explain that pull down lines are called vertical lines. Ask students to stand up straight. Point out that a vertical line might be drawn from the top of their head to the bottom of their feet. 
   * Have students look at letters H,D,E,t, b, i, 9, 4. Ask them what each have in common (vertical lines)
   * Model forming vertical lines in the air and have the students skywrite. 
* Practice:
   * Have students practice writing letters that have vertical lines appropriately on the paper. 
* Wrap-up/Recap: 
   * Use these questions for students to evaluate their writing:"What did we learn today? Is the stroke of your letter touching the right line on the paper (headline, midline, endline)?
Day 4: Review of  Writing Positions and Basic Strokes-Horizontal Lines (10 mins.)
* Review: 
   * Review with students the lines on the paper. 
* Model:  
   * Explain that side to side lines are called horizontal lines. Ask students to stand up straight. Point out that a vertical line might be drawn from the top of their head to the bottom of their feet. 
   * Have students look at letters F, G, B, z,f,e,5,7.  Ask them what each has in common (horizontal lines).
   * Model forming vertical lines in the air and have the students skywrite.


* Practice: Have students practice writing letters that have horizontal lines appropriately on the paper. 
* Wrap-up/Recap: 
   * Use these questions for students to evaluate their writing:"What did we learn today? Is the stroke of your letter touching the right line on the paper (headline, midline, endline)?
Day 5: Review of  Writing Positions and Basic Strokes-Circle Lines (10 mins.)
* Review: 
   * Review previously taught handwriting strokes.
   * Model:  
      * Model a backward circle line with the starting point at one o’clock. Model forming circle lines in the air as you say the stroke formation. Have students look at letters O, C, Q, e, c,d, q, 9.  Ask them what each have in common (circle lines). Forward circle lines- R, P, D, b, 5, 3
      * Model forming circle lines in the air and have the students skywrite. 
   * Practice:
      * Have students practice writing letters that have circle lines appropriately on the paper
* Wrap-up/Recap: 
   * Use these questions for students to evaluate their writing:Is the stroke of your letter touching the right line on the paper (headline, midline, endline)?
Differentiation:
Support:
* Create remediation packets/materials for students that need support forming specific letters. 
* For Letter Recognition/Formation: Provide pre-written dotted letters for tracing. Use play-doh or sand trays for tactile letter formation. Use multi-sensory activities (e.g., sky writing, tracing letters on a partner's back).
	Assessment: 
	Assessment (Weekly Assessment): (Independent Practice- possibly completed in small group- take notes using the Handwriting Behaviors Checklist)

	Before independent practice, meet with students in a small group to review community vocabulary using picture cards, photographs, and real-life examples.

rather than independently generated sentences.
	Students Approaching Independence
	Provide students with a simple newsletter planning organizer that includes:
• My Idea
• Newsletter Section
• Picture I Could Draw
Encourage students to discuss ideas with a partner before recording them. During conferences, prompt students to use vocabulary from the Concept Catcher and encourage them to add labels or words to their drawings. If handwriting difficulties occur, provide quick corrective feedback and opportunities to rewrite the word correctly.
	Students Who Are Independent
	Challenge students to contribute multiple ideas to newsletter sections and explain why each idea belongs there. Encourage students to add labels, captions, or additional community vocabulary to their work. Students may assist peers by explaining newsletter sections, modeling discussion expectations, or helping classmates locate vocabulary on the Concept Catcher. 
	ELL/Multilingual Learners
	Use photographs, gestures, picture cards, and real-life examples to teach community vocabulary. Allow students to discuss ideas with a partner before sharing with the class. Encourage students to use drawings, labels, and oral language to communicate ideas. Provide visual vocabulary cards for citizen, community, cooperate, volunteer, kindness, helper, and respect throughout the lesson. 
	Transcription Demands Addressed
	Because Week 1 of Writing Boot Camp focuses on handwriting and letter formation, transcription is taught explicitly during the lesson rather than treated solely as a support.
During the I DO, the teacher models correct pencil grip, posture, letter formation, spacing, and line placement using community vocabulary words. During the WE DO, students practice skywriting, tracing, and shared writing while receiving immediate feedback.
During the YOU DO, students independently write community vocabulary words and apply handwriting skills while contributing ideas to the Community Newsletter. The teacher circulates and provides targeted feedback on:
• Correct letter formation
• Starting points
• Letter size
• Line placement
• Spacing between words
• Pencil grip
Students who need additional support receive guided tracing, highlighted handwriting models, and teacher conferencing before independent writing. The goal is to build handwriting automaticity so transcription demands do not interfere with future planning, drafting, revising, and publishing tasks throughout the Community Newsletter unit.

SECTION 6: DIFFERENTIATION & TRANSCRIPTION SUPPORT
Students Needing Extended Scaffolds
	The teacher will meet with students in a small group to complete the graphic organizer together. Students will orally generate ideas before writing. During the Ready, Set, Write! Writing Boot Camp, students will receive additional support in identifying complete sentences versus fragments through teacher modeling, sentence sorting activities, and oral sentence rehearsal.
The teacher may ask guiding questions such as:
• Who is the sentence about?
• What is the subject doing?
• Is this a complete thought?
Sentence frames such as:
• A community garden helps ______.
• People work together by ______.
• The subject is ______.
• The predicate tells ______.
 The teacher may scribe student responses initially and gradually release responsibility as students gain confidence. Students will verbally rehearse complete sentences before writing.
Students Approaching Independence
Students will complete the graphic organizer independently but receive support during teacher conferences. During Writing Boot Camp activities, students will identify subjects and predicates in modeled sentences and practice correcting fragments.
The teacher will prompt students to think about sentence structure by asking:
• Does your sentence have a subject?
• Does your sentence have a predicate?
• Is your sentence complete?
Students will use sentence starters, anchor charts, and a checklist to monitor their work. Feedback will focus on writing complete sentences and adding supporting details.


	Students Approaching Independence
	Students will complete the planning organizer independently and receive support through teacher conferencing. During Writing Boot Camp, students will identify subjects and predicates in modeled sentences and practice correcting fragments.
Students will use:
• Sentence starters
• Anchor charts
• Editing checklist
• Word banks
Teacher feedback will focus on complete sentences, supporting details, and paragraph organization.




	Students Who Are Independent
	Students will independently plan, draft, revise, and edit their explanatory paragraphs.
During Writing Boot Camp, students will analyze more complex sentences, explain why sentences are complete, and identify subjects and predicates without support.
Students will be challenged to:
• Add additional supporting details
• Elaborate on ideas
• Include a concluding sentence
• Explain additional benefits of community gardens
Students may assist peers during collaborative discussions and planning activities.




	ELL/Multilingual Learners
	The teacher will preteach key vocabulary such as community, garden, neighbor, volunteer, teamwork, subject, predicate, sentence, and fragment using visuals and real-life examples.
During the Sentence Basics Writing Boot Camp, students will participate in partner discussions before writing to orally rehearse complete sentences. Visual word banks, sentence frames, and color-coded sentence examples will support language production.
Examples:
Subject = Families
Predicate = plant vegetables.
Students will practice identifying who or what the sentence is about and what action is happening before writing independently. During conferences, the teacher will model complete sentences and encourage students to use academic vocabulary from the lesson.


	Transcription Demands Addressed
	Because the focus of Week 2 is on explanatory writing and the Sentence Basics Writing Boot Camp, students will first organize their ideas orally and in a graphic organizer before writing. During Boot Camp, students will practice constructing complete sentences and identifying subjects and predicates before applying those skills to paragraph writing.
Anchor charts containing sentence examples, subject/predicate models, capitalization reminders, punctuation reminders, and high-frequency words will remain visible throughout the lesson.
During conferences, the teacher will address one or two transcription errors at a time so spelling and handwriting difficulties do not prevent students from expressing ideas. Students may use classroom word walls, vocabulary cards, sentence stems, and mentor text examples while drafting.
The goal is for students to develop automaticity in sentence construction so they can focus on explaining ideas clearly in their explanatory paragraphs.

	Before independent writing begins, meet with these students in a small teacher-led group. Review the Concept Catcher and community vocabulary using pictures and student-friendly language. Have students orally rehearse their ideas before writing by answering questions such as, "How can a good citizen help others?" and "What is one thing you can do in your community?"

• A good citizen helps by __________.
• I can help my community by __________.

If a student struggles to generate a sentence independently, use guided dictation. Ask the student to tell you their sentence while you repeat it back in complete form. Have the student echo the sentence several times before writing. For students with significant writing challenges, serve as a scribe for one sentence while encouraging them to independently write key vocabulary words. Reduce the amount of required writing to one complete sentence with a labeled illustration while maintaining the same learning goal. Encourage students to verbally rehearse their sentences with a partner before writing. During teacher conferences, ask guiding questions rather than supplying answers:
• What did the text teach us about citizens?
• Which vocabulary word could you add?
• Can you tell me more about that idea?
Provide sentence starters as needed but encourage students to complete the thought independently. Remind students to reread each sentence aloud to check whether it makes sense and sounds complete.


	Students Who Are Independent
	Challenge students to expand their newsletter contribution by adding multiple facts from the texts, creating captions for illustrations, writing additional sentences, or including examples from their own community. Encourage students to use two or more unit vocabulary words accurately.
Invite students to analyze how the mentor texts taught readers information. Ask:
• What facts did the author include?
• How can you teach your reader in the same way?
Students may also serve as peer coaches by listening to classmates rehearse sentences and asking questions that encourage elaboration.


	ELL/Multilingual Learners
	Begin with visual supports including photographs of community helpers, neighborhoods, schools, and volunteers. Explicitly teach vocabulary using gestures, pictures, and repeated oral practice.
Before writing, allow students to discuss ideas with a partner. Encourage students to explain their thinking verbally before expecting written responses. Model complete oral sentences and provide multiple opportunities for choral repetition.
Example:
Teacher: "A good citizen helps others."
Students repeat.
Teacher: "I can help my community by picking up trash."
Students repeat.
Provide vocabulary cards with pictures and allow students to reference them throughout the lesson. Accept drawings, labels, oral responses, and dictated responses as evidence of understanding when appropriate.


	Transcription Demands Addressed
	Because the purpose of this lesson is to communicate ideas about citizenship rather than assess spelling or handwriting, transcription demands are intentionally reduced. Students have access to a word wall containing unit vocabulary, anchor charts, sentence frames, and mentor text examples.
Before writing, students orally rehearse sentences multiple times with a partner or teacher. This reduces working-memory demands and allows students to focus on ideas. During conferencing, teachers help students stretch unfamiliar words, use environmental print, and locate words on the classroom word wall.
Students who struggle with handwriting may write fewer sentences while still demonstrating understanding through detailed illustrations, labels, oral explanations, or teacher-supported dictation. Feedback focuses first on content, vocabulary usage, and communication of ideas before addressing conventions, spelling, or handwriting.

Unit Essential Question:
How do artists express their feelings and ideas in their artwork?
	 
Unit Enduring Understandings
·        Artists draw inspiration from their imagination, feelings, and experiences.
·        One kind of art is painting, and artists use paint and medium in different ways.
·        Artists express themselves in diverse ways, even when painting portraits of others.
·        Writers follow a process (Analyze, Plan, Draft, Revise, Publish) to share their opinions clearly.
·        Opinions must be supported using text evidence, details, and information from words and pictures.
 
Unit Writing Product (End-of-Unit Writing)
Students will create an opinion response addressing the prompt: "Which portrait of Pepette do you think is the best one to hang on the wall of family portraits? Explain why, using information from the words and pictures."
The response will:
·        State a clear opinion answering the prompt.
·        Use text evidence, knowledge, and skills developed across modules.
·        Provide reasons supporting the opinion using information from words and pictures.
·        Use simple and compound sentences accurately.
·        Incorporate correct irregular verbs, possessive nouns, and subject-verb agreement.
·        Demonstrate correct foundational spelling patterns, final e, soft c/g, and three-letter blends.
 
Writing Focus Strands
☑  Critical Thinking / Integrated Literacy: Analyze artwork and stories, ask/answer questions, summarize text, describe story elements/structure, and extract key details from text and images.
☑  Writing Skills & Craft: Write opinion pieces; apply the process writing cycle: Analyze, Plan, Draft, Revise, and Publish.
☑  Syntax & Key Language Focus: Argue/Narrate using precise language. Master simple and compound sentences, irregular verbs, possessive nouns, and subject-verb agreement.
☑  Foundational Skills & Transcription: Decode/encode words with final e, soft c/g, three-letter blends (str, spl, spr, scr, shr, thr), long a (a, ai, ay, ea, eigh, ey), long e (e, ee, y, ea, ie, ey), and open syllable patterns.

Unit Modules & Reading Texts Sequence
• Module 1 (Sessions 1-9): Unit Opener & Foundations
Focuses on 'Creating Art' (Visual), 'Art Q&A' (Informational), 'Let's Paint!' (Informational), and 'Painting from With My Hands' (Poetry). Core skills: Notice & wonder, shared reading, vocabulary acquisition, identifying basic sentence mechanics.
• Module 2 (Sessions 10-16): Conceptual Exploration
Focuses on 'How Do Artists Create Art?' (Informational) and 'Oh, Olive!' (Fiction). Core skills: Understanding context clues, story element mapping, irregular verbs, and three-letter blends mapping.
• Module 3 (Sessions 17-24): Connections & Anchor Text
Focuses on 'Pictures and Portraits' (Informational), 'Emma and Muse' (Fiction), and the primary anchor text 'Painting Pepette' by Linda Ravin Lodding (Fiction). Core skills: Deep character analysis, tracking multi-text details, understanding possessives, and long vowel teams encoding.
• Module 4 (Sessions 25-30): Review & Process Writing Cycle
Focuses on the comprehensive End-of-Unit writing task. Core steps executed sequentially: Analyze the prompt -> Plan the response -> Draft -> Revise -> Publish.

How to persuade your readers and share your deep feelings!
O
	OPINION
	Tell how you feel! State your opinion clearly right at the start.
👉 Example: 'I think the first portrait of Pepette is the absolute best one to hang on the wall!'
	R
	REASON
	Why do you think that? Give a solid reason that supports your opinion.
👉 Example: 'This is because the painting uses bright, joyful colors that match her big personality.'
	E
	EXPLANATION / EVIDENCE
	Give details! Use facts and details from the text or illustrations to prove it.
👉 Example: 'In the story, Josette says she wants a portrait that is completely perfect and special.'
	O
	OPINION AGAIN
	Say it one more time! Wrap up your writing by restating your opinion in a brand new way.
👉 Example: 'That is why this beautiful portrait belongs on the family wall!'

Writing Task Description
	 Day 1: Self-Portrait & Personal Reflection
Students create a self-portrait that reflects their interests, personality, and experiences. After completing the portrait, students write 2–3 sentences explaining how their artwork represents them.
Students may respond to prompts such as:
* I am ______.
* My portrait shows ______.
* I included ______ because it is important to me.
Teacher conferences with students to support idea development, vocabulary use, and complete sentence formation.
Expected Student Product
* Self-portrait
* Written reflection consisting of 2–3 complete sentences
Day 2: Applying Regular Verbs
Students generate original sentences using action and thinking verbs related to art and creativity.
Students:
* Write at least two sentences containing action verbs.
* Write at least one sentence containing a thinking verb.
* Underline or highlight verbs within their writing.
Examples:
* I draw pictures after school.
* Artists paint colorful murals.
* I enjoy creating art projects.
Expected Student Product
* Three or more complete sentences demonstrating correct use of regular verbs
Day 3: Using Linking Words
Students combine ideas using linking words but, or, and so.
Students complete teacher-provided sentence frames and create original sentences that connect related ideas.
Examples:
* I like painting, but I also enjoy drawing.
* I can use crayons or markers.
* I enjoy art, so I practice often.
Students reread and revise writing to ensure ideas are connected clearly.
Expected Student Product
* Three complete sentences utilizing linking words correctly
Day 4: Subject-Verb Agreement
Students apply understanding of subject-verb agreement by correcting errors and generating original sentences.
Students:
* Review teacher-provided examples.
* Identify subjects and verbs.
* Correct errors when needed.
* Write original art-related sentences demonstrating correct agreement.
Examples:
* The artist paints a picture.
* Artists create beautiful artwork.
* My friends enjoy drawing.
Expected Student Product
* Corrected practice sentences
* Three original sentences demonstrating proper agreement
Day 5: Opinion Writing Launch
Students respond to the prompt:
My favorite kind of art is ______ because ______.
Students:
* State an opinion clearly.
* Provide at least one supporting reason.
* Use complete sentences.
* Apply grammar skills taught throughout the week.
Students ready for extension may:
* Add a second supporting reason.
* Include examples.
* Write a concluding sentence.
Expected Student Product
* Opinion statement
* Supporting reason(s)
* Complete sentence(s)

SECTION 6: DIFFERENTIATION & TRANSCRIPTION SUPPORT
Students Needing Extended Scaffolds
	Before Writing
• Meet with students in a teacher-led small group before independent writing begins.
• Revisit mentor text examples and discuss ideas orally before expecting students to write.
• Use pictures, artwork examples, and anchor charts to activate background knowledge.
• Review vocabulary from the Concept Catcher using visuals and student-friendly definitions.
• Encourage students to verbally explain ideas before writing them.
During Writing
• Provide sentence frames such as:
            * I think ______ because ______.
            * My favorite artwork is ______ because ______.
            * The artist ______.
            * Yesterday I ______.
• Use shared writing to model expectations before students write independently.
• Allow students to orally rehearse responses with a partner before writing.
• Break writing tasks into smaller chunks:
            * Step 1: Generate ideas.
            * Step 2: Complete organizer.
            * Step 3: Write one sentence.
            * Step 4: Add details.
• Reduce the amount of writing while maintaining the same learning objective.
• Allow dictation when generating ideas becomes a barrier.
Teacher Conferencing Focus
• Can the student explain an opinion verbally?
• Can the student identify a reason?
• Can the student use vocabulary from the unit?
• Does the student understand the task even if writing skills are still developing?


	Students Approaching Independence
	Before Writing
• Review anchor charts and mentor text examples.
• Have students discuss ideas with partners before drafting.
• Encourage students to use planning organizers independently.
During Writing
• Provide sentence starters rather than complete sentence frames.
• Encourage students to generate their own supporting details.
• Use checklists to help students monitor their own work.
• Prompt students to revisit mentor texts when they need support generating ideas.
Teacher Conferencing Focus
• Are students supporting opinions with reasons?
• Are students using linking words correctly?
• Are students applying grammar skills taught during the week?
• Are students organizing ideas logically?
Support for Revision
• Guide students in identifying places where more details could be added.
• Encourage students to reread writing for clarity.
• Provide targeted mini-lessons based on common errors observed during conferences.


	Students Who Are Independent
	During Writing
• Encourage students to provide multiple supporting reasons.
• Challenge students to elaborate using examples from mentor texts.
• Encourage students to make connections across multiple texts.
• Provide opportunities to extend writing beyond minimum expectations.
Extension Opportunities
• Write an additional opinion paragraph.
• Compare two types of artwork and explain a preference.
• Analyze how different artists communicate ideas.
• Serve as peer coaches during collaborative activities.
• Publish and present writing to classmates.
Teacher Conferencing Focus
• Are students elaborating effectively?
• Are students using precise vocabulary?
• Are students supporting opinions with multiple reasons and examples?
• Are students demonstrating independence throughout the writing process?


	ELL/Multilingual Learners
	Language Development
• Preteach academic vocabulary before each lesson.
• Use visuals, gestures, examples, and non-examples when introducing new terms.
• Connect vocabulary to students' personal experiences.
Oral Language Development
• Provide frequent Turn and Talk opportunities.
• Allow students to discuss ideas in their strongest language before writing.
• Encourage oral rehearsal before independent writing.
Writing Support
• Provide bilingual word banks when available.
• Pair students with supportive peers during collaborative activities.
• Offer sentence frames that gradually increase in complexity.
• Model expected language structures through shared writing.
Teacher Conferencing Focus
• Is the student able to explain ideas orally?
• Does the student understand the vocabulary?
• Does the student need additional language support before writing?


	Transcription Demands Addressed
	To ensure transcription demands do not interfere with idea generation, students will have access to sound walls, alphabet charts, vocabulary word banks, anchor charts, graphic organizers, and sentence stems throughout the week. Students will be encouraged to orally rehearse ideas before writing and will receive teacher support during planning, drafting, revising, and editing. Developmental spelling will be accepted during drafting, with conventions addressed during revision and editing lessons. Small-group instruction and teacher conferencing will provide targeted support for handwriting, spelling, capitalization, punctuation, and sentence construction while allowing students to focus primarily on communicating ideas.

	Day 1: Irregular Past-Tense Verbs
Revisit Learning Goal
• Say, "Today we will identify and use irregular past-tense verbs."
• Remind students that verbs are action words that tell what someone does, thinks, or feels.
• Explain that writers use past-tense verbs when writing about actions that already happened.
Explicit Instruction
• Review that regular past-tense verbs often end in -ed.
Examples:
            * paint → painted
            * brush → brushed
            * color → colored
• Explain that irregular past-tense verbs do not follow the -ed rule.
Display:
Present Tense
	Past Tense
	sit
	sat
	see
	saw
	make
	made
	give
	gave
	come
	came
	Think Aloud
Display:
The artist sits for a portrait.
The artist sat for a portrait yesterday.
Think Aloud:
"In the first sentence, sits is happening right now. That means it is present tense."
"In the second sentence, sat tells about something that already happened. Sat is the past tense of sit."
"Sat does not end in -ed. It is a different word, which means it is an irregular past-tense verb."
Additional Modeling
Display:
I see two portraits.
I saw three portraits last week.
Think Aloud:
"See is happening now."
"Saw already happened."
"Writers choose saw when they want readers to know the action happened in the past."
Connect to Writing
• Explain that authors often write about experiences, memories, and events that already happened.
• Tell students:
"If I am writing about visiting an art museum yesterday, I need past-tense verbs."
Model:
Yesterday I saw many paintings.
I made a sketch of my favorite portrait.
I gave my artwork to my teacher.

Day 2: Possessive Nouns
Writing Task Description
Students form possessive nouns and apply them in authentic writing.
Students will:
• Identify who owns an object in a sentence.
• Determine whether the noun is singular or plural.
• Add the appropriate apostrophe placement.
• Create original art-related sentences using possessive nouns.
Examples:
The artist's paintbrush is colorful.
The students' artwork is hanging in the hallway.
Teacher Conferencing Focus
• Does the student understand ownership?
• Can the student determine whether the noun is singular or plural?
• Is the apostrophe used correctly?
• Can the student explain their reasoning?

Students examine artwork and develop an opinion supported by reasons.

Which type of artwork do you think is most interesting?
Students will:
• Observe artwork examples.
• Record details they notice.
• Develop an opinion statement.
• Provide one or more supporting reasons.
• Use complete sentences.

Opinion
Linking Word
Reason
DAY 4 – WRITE A CONCLUSION
• Model adding a concluding statement.
• Think Aloud:
“A conclusion reminds the reader of my opinion and lets them know I am finished.”
• Example:
I think the first portrait is best because it has bright colors.
That is why I think it belongs on the family portrait wall.
DAY 5 – COMPLETE OPINION PIECE
• Model a complete response using the prompt.
• Demonstrate rereading, revising, and editing before publication.
• Review final success criteria.

SECTION 6: DIFFERENTIATION & TRANSCRIPTION SUPPORT
Students Needing Extended Scaffolds
	Students requiring intensive support will receive instruction in a teacher-led small group before independent writing. Visual supports, picture cards from Painting Pepette, and teacher modeling will be used to help students identify opinions, reasons, linking words, and conclusions. Students will verbally rehearse responses before writing and may dictate ideas to the teacher or a peer scribe when necessary.
Sentence frames will be provided throughout the week, such as:
• I think the _____ portrait is the best because _____.
• My reason is _____.
• That is why I think _____ is the best portrait.
Writing expectations may be reduced to one complete opinion statement, one supporting reason, and one concluding statement while maintaining grade-level learning targets. Frequent teacher conferencing and immediate corrective feedback will be provided.


	Students Approaching Independence
	Students approaching independence will use graphic organizers, anchor charts, and revision checklists to organize and strengthen their writing. Teachers will provide strategic prompting to encourage students to elaborate on reasons, incorporate details from the words and pictures, and revise for clarity.
Students will participate in peer discussions and partner conferences to rehearse ideas before writing. Additional teacher support will focus on helping students connect opinions and reasons using appropriate linking words and develop stronger conclusions.


	Students Who Are Independent
	Students demonstrating mastery will be encouraged to extend their writing by providing multiple supporting reasons, elaborating on evidence from the text and illustrations, and using precise vocabulary from the unit. Students may serve as peer coaches during collaborative writing activities and participate in mentor text analysis to identify effective opinion writing techniques.
Extension opportunities may include comparing multiple portraits, defending an opinion using additional evidence, or expanding the final response into a multi-paragraph piece.


	ELL/Multilingual Learners
	Multilingual learners will receive explicit vocabulary instruction using visuals, gestures, and real-world examples. Key vocabulary will be previewed and revisited throughout the week, including art, artist, portrait, canvas, imagination, expression, inspire, opinion, reason, and conclusion.
Students will have opportunities to discuss ideas orally before writing, use sentence frames, and work with supportive partners during collaborative activities. Visual anchor charts and bilingual resources will be available when appropriate to support comprehension and language development.


	Transcription Demands Addressed
	To ensure that handwriting, spelling, capitalization, and punctuation do not interfere with idea generation, students will have access to word banks, vocabulary cards, anchor charts, sentence frames, and graphic organizers. Oral rehearsal will be incorporated before writing tasks, and opportunities for shared writing, dictation, and teacher conferencing will be provided as needed.
Transcription skills will be reinforced during revision and editing while maintaining the primary focus on idea development, opinion writing structure, and evidence-based reasoning.

SECTION 6: DIFFERENTIATION & TRANSCRIPTION SUPPORT
Students Needing Extended Scaffolds
	Students requiring additional support will receive teacher-led small-group instruction during planning, drafting, revising, and editing. Graphic organizers will be partially completed when appropriate to reduce cognitive demands and help students focus on generating ideas. Sentence frames such as "I think ___ is the best portrait because ___" and "One reason is ___" will support sentence construction. Students will participate in oral rehearsal with partners before writing and may dictate ideas to a teacher or peer when needed. Frequent teacher check-ins and mini-lesson reteaching will be provided to reinforce opinion statements, supporting reasons, and use of evidence from both words and illustrations. 
	Students Approaching Independence
	Students approaching independence will use planning organizers, anchor charts, checklists, and peer conferences to support the writing process. Teacher feedback will focus on expanding reasons, incorporating evidence, and strengthening organization. These students will receive occasional prompts and guided questioning but will complete most writing tasks independently. Small-group support will be provided as needed during revision and editing. 
	Students Who Are Independent
	Students demonstrating independence will be encouraged to elaborate on their opinions by adding additional reasons, examples, or evidence from the text and illustrations. They may analyze mentor text features, serve as peer writing coaches, and extend their writing through cross-curricular connections. Independent writers may publish enhanced final drafts that include additional details, creative presentation features, or expanded explanations supporting their opinions. 
	ELL/Multilingual Learners
	Multilingual learners will receive visual vocabulary cards, bilingual word banks when available, illustrated sentence frames, and opportunities for structured partner talk before writing. Teachers will explicitly model academic vocabulary including folktale, fable, lesson, message, tradition, version, and origin. Students will rehearse oral responses using unit sentence frames before transferring ideas into written form. Anchor charts, gestures, illustrations, and mentor texts will provide contextual support for comprehension and language development. Peer partnerships will encourage discussion and clarification of ideas throughout the writing process. 
	Transcription Demands Addressed
	Transcription demands are intentionally addressed separately from idea generation so students can focus first on developing meaningful narratives. During planning and drafting, students may use invented spelling while generating ideas. Word walls, vocabulary banks, mentor texts, and anchor charts remain available throughout instruction. Oral rehearsal opportunities help students formulate complete sentences before writing. Editing lessons explicitly address capitalization, punctuation, spacing, spelling, past-tense verb usage, and correct use of reflexive pronouns. Teacher conferencing provides individualized support for handwriting, sentence construction, and conventions. Students use the Narrative Writing Checklist to monitor writing expectations and ensure transcription skills do not interfere with communicating ideas effectively.

Unit Essential Question:
How do living things survive in a desert habitat?
Georgia Standards Addressed
2.T.T.2.c Use knowledge of expository techniques to create texts that introduce a topic, use facts and definitions to supply information about the topic, and provide a concluding statement or section.
K-12.P.EICC.4.g Make changes to the text based on self-evaluation or external feedback, revising the organization, ideas,information, word choices, and craft techniques in order to increase the text’s effectiveness.
K-2.L.GC.1: Grammar, Usage, & Mechanics
Uses correct subject and verb agreement in sentence construction.
Form and use the past tense of irregular verbs. 
Use adjectives and adverbs.
K-2.L.GC.1: Grammar, Usage, & Mechanics
Use periods, exclamation marks, and question marks at the end of sentences.
Use commas to separate items in a series and to format dates, addresses, salutations, and closings.
2.L.GC.2.b : Use a variety of simple and compound sentences (i.e., declarative, imperative, interrogative, and exclamatory) to develop clarity and coherence in written texts.
 Unit Enduring Understandings
• Desert habitats contain unique plants and animals that have special adaptations that help them survive.
• Plants and animals depend on their environment to meet their needs for food, water, and shelter.
• Informational texts help readers learn about the characteristics and survival strategies of living things.
• Writers gather information from multiple sources and organize facts to explain a topic clearly.
• Explanatory writing uses facts, details, comparisons, and evidence from texts to teach readers about a topic.
Unit Writing Product (End-of-Unit Writing)
After reading "A Day and Night in the Desert" and "Cactus Hotel," students will complete an explanatory essay addressing the prompt:
"Explain how living things survive in the desert. Compare and contrast specific facts from 'A Day and Night in the Desert' and 'Cactus Hotel' in your response."
The written response will:
• Clearly explain how plants and animals survive in a desert habitat.
• Compare and contrast information from both texts.
• Use facts, details, and examples gathered throughout the unit.
• Include an introduction, supporting details, and a concluding statement.
• Use simple and compound sentences appropriately.
• Incorporate descriptive adjectives and correctly use irregular verbs.
• Demonstrate correct capitalization, punctuation, commas in a series, and foundational spelling patterns.
Writing Focus Strands
☑ Critical Thinking / Integrated Literacy: Analyze informational texts, compare and contrast information across sources, identify key details, ask and answer questions, and explain how living things adapt to their environment.
☑ Writing Skills & Craft: Write explanatory pieces using information gathered from multiple texts; organize ideas using an introduction, supporting details, and conclusion; apply the writing process cycle: Analyze, Plan, Draft, Revise, and Publish.
☑ Syntax & Key Language Focus: Explain information using precise academic language. Develop sentence variety through simple and compound sentences while applying adjectives and irregular verbs appropriately.
☑ Foundational Skills & Transcription: Apply grade-level spelling patterns, punctuation, capitalization, commas in a series, and accurate encoding/decoding skills while composing informational writing.
Unit Vocabulary
Unit Concept Vocabulary:
desert, habitat, survive, adaptation
Key Vocabulary:
cactus, shelter, predator, prey, nocturnal, burrow, environment, camouflage, moisture, drought, desert animal, desert plant, adaptation, protection, survival
Academic Vocabulary:
compare, contrast, key details, summarize, informational text, text evidence, topic, introduction, conclusion, explanation, adjective, irregular verb, commas in a series, process writing, analyze, plan, draft, revise, publish
Unit Modules & Reading Texts Sequence
• Module 1 (Sessions 1–9): Unit Opener & Habitat Foundations: Introduces desert habitats, environmental conditions, and survival needs of plants and animals. Core skills: activating knowledge, asking and answering questions, vocabulary development, and identifying key details.
• Module 2 (Sessions 10–16): Conceptual Exploration: Focuses on understanding desert adaptations and informational text structures. Texts include "A Day and Night in the Desert." Core skills: summarizing, identifying text features, gathering facts, and understanding descriptive language.
• Module 3 (Sessions 17–24): Connections & Anchor Texts: Focuses on comparing information across texts and examining relationships between living things and their environment. Texts include "Cactus Hotel." Core skills: compare/contrast, text evidence collection, analyzing details, and explaining survival strategies.
• Module 4 (Sessions 25–30): Review & Process Writing Cycle: Focuses on the comprehensive End-of-Unit explanatory writing task. Core steps executed sequentially: Analyze the prompt → Plan the response → Draft → Revise → Publish. Core skills: synthesizing information from multiple texts, organizing explanatory writing, revising for clarity, and editing conventions.

U3 Writing Sample
Desert Habitat Survival
Living things survive in the desert because they have special adaptations. Plants and animals need food, water, and shelter to live in the hot, dry desert. The texts "A Day and Night in the Desert" and "Cactus Hotel" explain different ways living things survive.
In "A Day and Night in the Desert," many animals survive by staying safe and finding food. Some animals come out at night when the desert is cooler. Others live in burrows to stay out of the hot sun. These adaptations help animals survive in the harsh desert environment.
In "Cactus Hotel," the saguaro cactus helps many living things survive. Birds, insects, and other animals use the cactus for food and shelter. The cactus stores water, which helps it live during dry times. This text shows how one plant can support many animals.
Both texts explain how living things survive in the desert. However, "A Day and Night in the Desert" focuses on many different desert animals, while "Cactus Hotel" focuses on one cactus and the animals that depend on it. Both texts teach that plants and animals have adaptations that help them live in a desert habitat.
Living things survive in the desert because they have special adaptations. The facts from both texts helped me understand how plants and animals meet their needs in a hot, dry environment.

Section 4: Lesson Sequence — Gradual Release of Responsibility
	I DO — Teacher Modeling (Explicit Instruction)
	Skill / Strategy Named
	Explanatory writers introduce their topic with a clear TOPIC SENTENCE, then use KEY DETAILS — facts and definitions — to explain. They use precise ADJECTIVES to make descriptions specific and vivid. They cite TEXT EVIDENCE — information from what they've read — not personal opinion.
	Think-Aloud / Demonstration
	Day 1
Display the Desert Habitat visual. Introduce the unit topic and explain that writers build knowledge before writing. Model observing the visual and recording observations on a Notice and Wonder chart. Introduce the class project, A Visitor's Guide to the Desert, and explain that students will become experts on a desert plant or animal and teach others about how it survives in the desert.
Day 2
Display the Desert Habitat visual and model using precise adjectives to describe what is observed. Compare vague words such as hot and dry with more precise words such as scorching, arid, rocky, and sparse. Create a class anchor chart of descriptive vocabulary that will be used throughout the unit.
Day 3
Read At Home in the Desert (Read 1). Model identifying the topic sentence and locating supporting details that explain the main idea. Demonstrate how informational texts are organized around a main idea supported by facts and details.
Day 4
Read At Home in the Desert (Read 2). Model determining the author's purpose by examining the information presented in the text. Demonstrate how readers use evidence from the text to explain why an author wrote a piece of informational writing.
Day 5
Model writing strong explanatory topic sentences. Compare weak and strong examples and explain how effective topic sentences introduce the topic while providing the reader with the main idea of the paragraph. Create a topic sentence anchor chart for future reference.


	Craft Move Highlighted
	Explanatory writers use PRECISE ADJECTIVES to create a clear picture for their reader. 'The desert is hot' is vague. 'The Sonoran Desert reaches scorching temperatures of 120°F, baking the cracked, sandy ground' is PRECISE. Three adjectives that are specific and content-connected beat ten vague ones.
	Anchor Chart / Visual Created
	Chart 1: 'Explanatory Writing Structure' — Topic Sentence (names the topic + key idea) → Key Detail 1 (fact or definition) → Key Detail 2 (fact with adjective) → Key Detail 3 (cause-effect connection) → Concluding Sentence. Chart 2: 'Desert Vocabulary Web' — habitat, desert, survive, ecosystem, adapt — with definitions and example sentences. Unit vocabulary wall started: harsh, scorching, unique, ecosystem, adaptation.

Section 4: Lesson Sequence — Gradual Release of Responsibility
	I DO — Teacher Modeling (Explicit Instruction)
	Skill / Strategy Named
	Explanatory writers use ADVERBS to explain HOW, WHEN, or WHERE something happens. 'The fennec fox hunts silently at night' is more informative than 'the fennec fox hunts.' They also COMPARE AND CONTRAST key details from multiple texts to deepen their explanation — noting where two texts agree, where they differ, and what they each add.
	Think-Aloud / Demonstration
	Day 1
Read Fennec Foxes (Read 1). Model reading like a writer by identifying the topic sentence, adjectives, adverbs, and cause-and-effect language. Demonstrate how authors organize information to explain an animal's adaptation and survival.
Day 2
Read Fennec Foxes (Read 2). Model drafting an explanatory paragraph about one fennec fox adaptation using text evidence. Demonstrate how to create a topic sentence and support it with key details from the text.
Day 3
Read Gila Monster's Burrow (Read 1). Model comparing and contrasting information from two texts. Identify similarities and differences between how the fennec fox and gila monster survive in the desert.
Day 4
Read Gila Monster's Burrow (Read 2). Model strengthening explanatory sentences by adding adverbs and precise language. Demonstrate how cause-and-effect language helps explain why an adaptation is important for survival.
Day 5
Model peer conferring using the 2-Glow/1-Grow protocol. Demonstrate how to use the Explanatory Writing Checklist to revise and edit a paragraph for clarity, conventions, and completeness.


	Craft Move Highlighted
	Explanatory writers use ADVERBS to add precision to their explanations. 'The Gila monster stores fat efficiently in its thick tail' — the adverb 'efficiently' tells HOW it stores fat, which makes the explanation more complete. Find an adverb in Fennec Foxes and borrow it for your own paragraph!
	Anchor Chart / Visual Created
	Chart 5: 'Comparing Two Texts — Same Topic, Different Details' — T-chart with Fennec Foxes vs. Gila Monster's Burrow: Similar (both burrow, both desert, both nocturnal) / Different (diet, appearance, specific adaptations). Chart 6: 'Explanatory Writing Checklist' — 7 items for self-editing.

	I DO — Teacher Modeling (Explicit Instruction)
	Skill / Strategy Named
	Published writers choose their clearest, most evidence-rich paragraph for publication. They revise specifically for CONCLUDING STATEMENT strength — the conclusion should restate the topic using different words and leave the reader with the key insight. Compare-contrast writing requires SPECIFIC TEXT CITATION — naming the text and giving the exact detail.

End-of-Unit Writing Prompt: 'Explain how living things survive in the desert. Compare facts from A Day and Night in the Desert and Cactus Hotel in your response.'
	Writing Focus for This Text
	Students use BOTH texts as content sources. Key strategies for the process writing: (1) EXPLAIN how living things survive — this requires at least one cause-effect explanation from each text; (2) COMPARE — find at least one way both texts agree on survival strategies AND one way they present different information; (3) CITE — use the author's name or book title when introducing evidence. The strongest responses will organize their writing as: Introduction (topic sentence) → Explanation from Text 1 → Explanation from Text 2 → Compare-Contrast Connection → Conclusion (restates topic + broader significance). Both authors' purposes are to INFORM — but they do so through DIFFERENT organizational lenses.

Unit Writing Product (End-of-Unit Writing)
After reading "Yellowstone" and "Tree Speaks," students will complete an opinion essay addressing the prompt: "Which national park would you rather visit: Yellowstone National Park or the Grand Canyon? Name one of the poem's words or phrases that helped you decide, and explain how it helped you."
The written response will:
·        State a clear opinion answering the prompt detailing which park they prefer to visit.
·        Use explicit text evidence, knowledge, and descriptive language skills developed across modules.
·        Provide reasons supporting the opinion using specific information from words, poetry, and informational text features.
·        Master and use simple and compound sentences accurately to argue/inform.
·        Incorporate correct language conventions including subject-verb agreement, present/past-tense verbs, and correct usage of adjectives and adverbs.
·        Demonstrate accurate foundational spelling patterns, decoding/encoding words with r-controlled vowels, diphthongs (ou, ow), consonant +le syllable patterns, comparative endings (-er, -est), and suffixes (-ful, -less, -y, -ly).
Writing Focus Strands
☑  Critical Thinking / Integrated Literacy: Analyze informational and literary text (poetry), ask and answer questions, summarize text, describe features of poetry, explain figurative language, and extract key details from text features and images.
☑  Writing Skills & Craft: Write structured opinion pieces; gather and recall information from multi-text sources; use technology to publish; apply the process writing cycle: Analyze, Plan, Draft, Revise, and Publish.
☑  Syntax & Key Language Focus: Argue and inform using precise academic language. Master simple and compound sentences, past/present tense verbs, subject-verb agreement, and targeted language use of adjectives and adverbs.
☑  Foundational Skills & Transcription: Decode and encode longer words with r-controlled vowels (er, ir, ur, or, ar, oar, ore, ear, eer, ere, are, air), diphthongs (ou, ow), consonant +le syllable patterns, comparative endings (-er, -est), suffixes (-ful, -less, -y, -ly), and read texts with accuracy and fluency.

Use the delicious O-R-E-O strategy to write your paragraph!

[O] OPINION — Say it one more time! 🎉

	Skill / Strategy Named
	Writing Descriptive Sentences with Similes
	Think-Aloud / Demonstration
	Day 1
Read Who Has Seen the Wind? and model identifying similes and figurative language. Demonstrate how poets help readers create mental images by comparing one thing to another using like and as.
Day 2
Model creating original similes inspired by nature and national park scenes. Demonstrate how similes make descriptions more vivid and help readers picture what the writer sees.
Day 3
Read Hide and Seek and model identifying sensory language and descriptive word choices. Demonstrate how poets use vivid adjectives to create strong images in the reader's mind.
Day 4
Use a photograph of a national park scene to model writing descriptive sentences that combine vivid adjectives and similes. Demonstrate how figurative language strengthens descriptive writing.
Day 5
Model revising descriptive writing by improving adjectives, strengthening similes, and rereading for rhythm and flow. Demonstrate how writers choose words carefully to create a clear picture for readers.


	Mentor Text Used
	"Who Has Seen the Wind?" by Christina Rossetti — Connection Text, Sessions 5–6
	Craft Move Highlighted
	Simile construction: "___ is like ___" or "___ as ___ as ___"
	Anchor Chart / Visual Created
	Anchor Chart #2: "Simile Superpower!" — illustrated chart with nature simile examples and a blank frame for students to fill
	🤝 WE DO — Guided Practice (Shared / Interactive Writing)
	Shared Writing 




Activity
	Day 1
Students identify similes and figurative language in Who Has Seen the Wind? and discuss what images the poet creates.
Day 2

Day 3
Students identify sensory words and vivid adjectives in Hide and Seek. The class discusses how these words help readers visualize the scene.
Day 4
Students participate in shared writing using a photograph of Old Faithful or another national park scene. Together, the class creates descriptive sentences that include vivid adjectives and similes.
Day 5
Students work with partners to revise shared writing by improving word choice, adding stronger similes, and discussing how descriptive language affects the reader.

	Skill / Strategy Named
	Organizing Informational Writing: Topic → Details → Closing
	Think-Aloud / Demonstration
	Day 1
Introduce U.S. National Parks: Yellowstone National Park. Model identifying the author's purpose and explaining how informational texts teach readers about real places. Demonstrate how headings, photographs, and text features help readers gather information.
Day 2
Model using text features such as headings, charts, captions, and photographs to locate important information about Yellowstone National Park. Demonstrate how readers use these features to find key details efficiently.
Day 3
Model selecting the most important facts from the text. Demonstrate how informational writers choose relevant details instead of including every fact they learn. Record selected facts on a graphic organizer.
Day 4
Model organizing information into an informational paragraph using a topic sentence, supporting details, and a closing sentence. Demonstrate how each detail connects back to the main topic.
Day 5
Model revising and editing an informational paragraph by checking that all details support the topic sentence, improving word choice, and strengthening the closing sentence.

Students participate in sorting Yellowstone facts into categories such as important details and less important details. The class discusses which details would be most helpful in an informational paragraph.
Day 4
Students help complete a shared hamburger graphic organizer and contribute ideas for a class informational paragraph about Yellowstone National Park.

Students participate in a shared revision lesson by reviewing the class paragraph and checking for a clear topic sentence, strong supporting details, and an effective closing sentence.

UNIT 5 OVERVIEW
Tales and Fables: Lessons from Around the World
Grade:

Unit Essential Question:
	What can we learn from folktales and fables?
	 
Georgia Standards Addressed
2.T.T.1.e:  Use knowledge of narrative techniques (e.g., characters, settings, events, dialogue) to create texts that recount real or imagined experiences and events with a sense of closure.


K-12.P.EICC.4.g:  Make changes to the text based on self-evaluation or external feedback, revising the organization, ideas, information, word choices, and craft techniques in order to increase the text’s effectiveness.


    STANDARD K-2.L.GC.1: Grammar, Usage, & Mechanics
    Learn and apply conventions of Standard English grammar, usage, and mechanics to aid the 
    comprehension of texts and to communicate clearly in written and spoken language.
   (Reflexive pronouns, consistent verb tense, expanding and rearranging sentences)
      Demonstrate command of capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.
     (Diphthongs oi/oy, variant vowels, contractions, irregular plurals, compound words, vowel-team
      syllable patterns)
 
Unit Enduring Understandings
·        Folktales and fables are traditional stories that have been retold all over the world to share cultural values and teach life lessons.
·        Different versions of traditional stories are shared across different cultures, showcasing both universal morals and unique perspectives.
·        Fables and folktales often feature distinct structural patterns (like short plots, animal characters, or explicit central messages) that guide readers toward a moral.
·        Writers follow a structured process cycle (Analyze, Plan, Draft, Revise, Publish) to compose well-elaborated narratives with clear event sequences.
·        Narratives are enhanced by expanding and rearranging sentences and using descriptive details to illustrate characters' actions, thoughts, and feelings.
 
Unit Writing Product (End-of-Unit Writing)
After reading several folktales and fables including "The Little Red Ant and the Great Big Crumb," students will complete a narrative writing task addressing the prompt: "Write your own story with at least two events that also teaches the lesson 'You can do it if you think you can.' Be sure to describe the characters' thoughts or feelings in each event."
The written response will:
·        Recount a well-elaborated narrative containing at least two sequential events that explicitly teach the given lesson.
·        Use text evidence, knowledge of fable structures, and descriptive language skills developed across modules.
·        Incorporate descriptions of the characters' specific actions, internal thoughts, and feelings across each event.
·        Master and use expanded and rearranged simple and compound sentences accurately to narrate and inform.
·        Incorporate correct language conventions including consistent verb tense, reflexive pronouns, and standard capitalization/punctuation.
·        Demonstrate accurate foundational spelling patterns, decoding/encoding words with diphthongs (oi, oy), variant vowels (oo, ou, u, u_e, ew, ue, aw, au, a(l)), short vowel digraphs (ea, ou, y), vowel-team syllable patterns, contractions, irregular plurals, and compound words.
 
Writing Focus Strands
☑  Critical Thinking / Integrated Literacy:  Analyze informational texts, folktales, and fables; ask and answer questions; summarize text; retell stories and explain their central message, lesson, or moral; describe story structure; compare and contrast stories; and identify characters' perspectives.
☑  Writing Skills & Craft:  Write structured narrative pieces; plan, revise, and edit text; use temporal words to signal event order; use technology to publish; apply the process writing cycle: Analyze, Plan, Draft, Revise, and Publish.
☑  Syntax & Key Language Focus:  Narrate and inform using precise language. Use reflexive pronouns, maintain consistent verb tense, and master expanding and rearranging simple and compound sentences.
☑  Foundational Skills & Transcription:  Decode and encode words with diphthongs (oi, oy), variant vowels (oo, ou, u, u_e, ew, ue, aw, au, a(l)), short vowel digraphs (ea, ou, y), contractions, irregular plurals, compound words, vowel-team syllable patterns, and read texts with accuracy and fluency.
 
Unit Vocabulary
Unit Concept Vocabulary:
	"folktale, origin, tradition, version"
	Key Vocabulary:
	"lessons, message, wheat, landed, grind, bragged, contest, discouraged, hare, tortoise, steady, truce, mend, alarmed, ceremony, pounced, crumb, dreadful"
	Academic Vocabulary:
	"summarize, key details, ask and answer questions, retell, central message, moral, lesson, story structure, character perspective, compare, contrast, reflexive pronouns, past/present/future tense, dialogue, narrative, temporal words, conclusion, process writing, analyze, plan, draft, revise, publish"
	 
Unit Modules & Reading Texts Sequence
Module 1 (Sessions 1-10): Unit Opener & Knowledge Building: Focuses on introductory concepts of folktales, fables, and retelling core elements. Texts include: Unit Media (Visual Text), 'A World of Stories' (Visual Text), 'What Are Folktales and Fables?' (Conceptual/Informational Text), 'The Little Red Hen: An Old Fable' by Heather Forrest (Connection Text/Fable), and 'The Contest Between the Sun and the Wind: An Aesop's Fable' by Heather Forrest (Connection Text/Fable). Core skills: Notice & wonder, activating knowledge, summarizing text, determining word meaning, explaining central messages, retelling stories, using reflexive pronouns, regular/irregular verb tenses, and decoding/encoding diphthongs (oi, oy) and variant vowels (oo, ou, u).
Module 2 (Sessions 11-17): Conceptual Exploration & Geographies: Focuses on comparing story variations, expanding sentence structure, and exploring fables. Texts include: 'The Hare and the Tortoise' by Val Biro (Genre: Fable) and 'When Turtle Grew Feathers: A Folktale from the Choctaw Nation' by Tim Tingle (Genre: Folktale). Core skills: Retelling stories, describing story structure, explaining central messages, understanding character perspectives, comparing/contrasting narratives, using contractions, expanding/rearranging sentences, and encoding/decoding variant vowels (oo, ou, u, u_e, ew, ue, aw, au, a(l)).
Module 3 (Sessions 18-24): Connections & Anchor Texts: Focuses on advanced narrative comprehension, cross-text thematic links, and dialogue features. Texts include: 'The Silly Chicken' by Idries Shah (Genre: Folktale), 'Mabela the Clever' by Margaret Read MacDonald (Genre: Folktale), and 'The Little Red Ant and the Great Big Crumb: A Mexican Fable' by Shirley Climo (Anchor Text/Fable). Core skills: Asking/answering complex text-dependent questions, identifying story structures, using consistent verb tenses, tracking characters' perspectives, understanding dialogue, and mastering variant vowels (aw, au, a(l)) and short vowel digraphs (ea, ou, y).
Module 4 (Sessions 25-30): Review & Process Writing Cycle: Focuses on the comprehensive End-of-Unit narrative process writing task through a dedicated 'Flex/Review Week' and explicit process writing blocks. Core steps executed sequentially: Analyze the prompt -> Plan the response -> Draft -> Revise -> Publish. Core skills: Synthesis of multi-text structural knowledge, constructing an original narrative with character details (thoughts, feelings, actions) and a clear moral, peer/instructor editing, and comprehensive review of all Unit 5 foundational skills (diphthongs, variant vowels, short vowel digraphs, contractions, compound words).

U5 Writing Sample
The Little Rabbit Believed in Himself
One day, a little rabbit wanted to jump across a small stream. The stream looked wide, and the rabbit felt nervous. He thought, "What if I fall into the water?" The rabbit told himself that he was not strong enough. He sat on a rock and watched the water move.
Soon, a turtle walked by. The turtle said, "You can do it if you keep trying." The rabbit thought about the turtle's words. He told himself to be brave. Then he took a deep breath and jumped. He landed safely on the other side of the stream. The rabbit felt proud of himself because he did not give up.
The rabbit learned that you can do it if you think you can. After that day, he believed in himself whenever he faced a challenge.


























































Myself and the Mountain
One day, a rabbit wanted to climb a tall hill. He looked at the top and felt nervous. He said to himself, “I am too small to climb that hill.” The rabbit started walking anyway.
As he climbed, he became tired. He almost turned around and went home. Then he reminded himself that he could do hard things if he kept trying. He took a deep breath and kept climbing.
At last, the rabbit reached the top of the hill. He looked at the beautiful view and felt proud of himself. He learned that believing in yourself can help you do difficult things.
Lesson: You can do it if you think you can.

Unit 6 Overview
UNIT 6 OVERVIEW
Earth's Water and Systems
Grade:
	2
	Writing Type:
	Explanatory Writing
	Unit Length:
	4 Modules (30 Sessions / Weeks vary by implementation)
	 
Unit Essential Question:
	How are humans and water connected?
	Georgia Standards Addressed
·        2.T.T.2.d: Use knowledge of expository techniques to create texts that introduce a topic, use facts and definitions to develop the topic, and provide a concluding statement or section. (Adapted for explanatory focus)
·        K-12.P.EICC.4.g: Make changes to the text based on self-evaluation or external feedback, revising the organization, ideas, information, word choices, and craft techniques in order to increase the text’s effectiveness. (Aligned across units)
·       K-2.L.GC.1: Learn and apply conventions of Standard English grammar, usage, and mechanics to aid the comprehension of texts and to communicate clearly in written and spoken language.
 (Verb tenses, , capitalization, commas in letters)
·       K-2.L.GC.2b: Use a variety of simple and compound sentences (including a variety of sentence types) to develop clarity and coherence in written texts. (expanding and combining, compound sentences)
           ·   2.L.V.2.c Construct words using frequently occurring root words and affixes. (prefixes, suffixes)
      ·  2.F.P.3.a: Encode regularly spelled two-syllable words with a variety of spelling patterns (VVCC,
        VVCe, VCCC, VVCCC) by applying knowledge of basic phonics skills, including high-frequency 
        words.


Unit Enduring Understandings
·        Water moves in different ways and exists in different forms across our planet.
·        Solid water (glaciers) impacts and shapes the land in unique, powerful ways.
·        Bodies of water are interconnected to each other and deeply connected to human life.
·        Writers follow a structured process (Analyze, Plan, Draft, Revise, Publish) to share information clearly.
·        Explanatory text must be supported using clear facts, definitions, and details from multiple texts, photos, and diagrams.
Unit Writing Product (End-of-Unit Writing)
Students will create an explanatory response addressing the prompt: "Moving water changes the landscape it runs through. Use two facts from Follow the Water from Brook to Ocean to describe the connection between moving water and the changes it makes to the land."
The response will:
·        Introduce the topic clearly and state an informative focus answering the prompt.
·        Use text evidence, facts, definitions, and knowledge developed across modules.
·        Provide specific reasons and descriptions supporting the connection between water and land changes.
·        Accurately use, expand, and rearrange simple and compound sentences.
·        Incorporate correct grammar conventions for verb tenses (past, present, future, and perfect).
·        Demonstrate correct command of punctuation (commas in letters/lists) and foundational word patterns (syllables, inflections, prefixes, and suffixes).
Writing Focus Strands
☑  Critical Thinking / Integrated Literacy:  Analyze informational text, graphics, and visual media; ask and answer questions; summarize text; identify author's purpose; describe connections between scientific concepts/ideas; and extract key details from text and images.
☑  Writing Skills & Craft:  Write informative/explanatory texts; apply the process writing cycle: Analyze, Plan, Draft, Revise, and Publish; research, take notes, and gather information from multiple sources.
☑  Syntax & Key Language Focus:  Inform and explain using precise, academic language. Master expanding and rearranging simple and compound sentences, correct application of verb tenses, and use of commas.
☑  Foundational Skills & Transcription:  Decode/encode words with syllable patterns (closed, open, final e, final stable syllables -sion, -tion, -le, -el, -al), r-controlled vowels, vowel teams, inflectional endings, prefixes (re-, pre-, un-, dis-), and suffixes (-er, -or, -ly, -y, -ful, -less, -ion). Read texts with accuracy and fluency.
Unit Vocabulary
Unit Concept Vocabulary:
	body of water, cycle, shore, system
	Key Vocabulary:
	salt water, fresh water, survival, reservoirs, pollute, landform, churns, recede, gorge, friction, ice crystals, sediment, flow, retreat, cozy, crumble, tide pool, jumbled, plankton, algae, springs, bank, mouth, delta
	Academic Vocabulary:
	summarize, key details, present/past/future/perfect tense verbs, adjectives, compare, contrast, direct address, author's purpose, point, reasons, greeting, closing, body of letter, explanatory writing, topic, facts, problem, solution, definition, sequence of events, cause, effect, concluding statement, research, paraphrase
	Unit Modules & Reading Texts Sequence
•  Module 1 (Sessions 1-10): Unit Opener & Foundations:  Focuses on 'Unit Media' (Visual Text), 'Water on the Move' (Visual Text), 'Water, Water Everywhere!' (Conceptual/Informational Text), and 'What's So Fresh About Fresh Water?' (Connection/Informational Text), and 'Waterfalls' (Connection/Informational Text). Core skills: Notice & wonder, activate and build knowledge, shared reading, summarizing text, asking and answering questions, identifying body of water cycles, irregular verbs usage, and closed/open/final e syllable patterns parsing.
•  Module 2 (Sessions 11-16): Conceptual Exploration:  Focuses on 'Glaciers' (Connection/Informational Text) and 'Glacier on the Move' (Connection/Narrative Nonfiction). Core skills: Identifying author's purpose, determining word meaning using context clues, describing cause/effect connections, mastering verb tenses, and decoding r-controlled vowels and final stable syllables (-sion, -tion, -iron).
•  Module 3 (Sessions 17-24): Connections & Anchor Text:  Focuses on 'Seashore and Tides' (Connection/Informational Text), 'One Small Place By the Sea' (Connection/Narrative Nonfiction), and the primary anchor text 'Follow the Water from Brook to Ocean' by Arthur Dorros (Informational Text). Core skills: Tracking connections across texts, analyzing multi-text details, understanding cause/effect of moving water, writing comma-separated lists/letters, and mapping vowel team syllables.
•  Module 4 (Sessions 25-30): Review & Process Writing Cycle:  Focuses on the comprehensive End-of-Unit explanatory writing task. Core steps executed sequentially across the Flex Week process: Analyze the prompt -> Plan the response -> Draft -> Revise -> Publish. Accompanied by integrated Unit 6 assessments for foundational skills and literacy.

Vocabulary Word

	body of water
	A large area of water, such as a lake, river, or ocean.

	cycle
	A series of things that happen over and over in the same order.
	As part of the water cycle, rain falls to Earth.
	shore
	The land right next to a body of water.
	We collected seashells along the shore at the beach.
	system
	A group of parts that work together to do something.
