U6 Writing Sample
Unit 6 Writing Sample
Water on the Move
How are moving water and changes to land connected?
Moving water can change the land in many ways. As water travels from a brook to an ocean, it shapes the land around it. Water is important because it helps create and change landforms over time.
In Follow the Water from Brook to Ocean, the author explains that water flows from small streams into larger bodies of water. As the water moves, it carries sediment. This sediment can be moved to new places and change the shape of the land.
The text also explains that water can create landforms such as deltas. When water slows down near the mouth of a river, sediment is left behind. Over time, this process changes the land and creates new areas of soil.
Moving water and changes to land are connected because water is constantly shaping Earth's surface. The facts from the text helped me understand how water moves and changes the land around us.

🌊 OUR WRITING JOURNEY! 🌊
How to Write an Explanatory Piece
Essential Question: How are humans and water connected?
🧠 STEP 1: ANALYZE
	Read the prompt carefully! What is it asking us to explain? Look at your texts like Follow the Water from Brook to Ocean and look for clues!
	✏️ STEP 2: PLAN
	Gather facts & evidence! Take clear notes about how moving water changes the land. Use a graphic organizer to sort your ideas before writing.
	📝 STEP 3: DRAFT
	Write it out! Put your ideas into complete simple and compound sentences. Use your vocabulary words like body of water, cycle, erosion, and stream!
	🔍 STEP 4: REVISE
	Make it better! Rearrange sentences to make sense. Add juicy details, check your verb tenses (past, present, future), and use neat transition words!
	🚀 STEP 5: PUBLISH
	Share your masterpiece! Copy it in your best handwriting or type it up cleanly. Celebrate your hard work as an expert writer! 🎉

	Think-Aloud / Demonstration
	 Day 1
Skill / Strategy Named
Explaining Connections Between Bodies of Water
Think-Aloud / Demonstration
"In informational writing, authors explain how ideas are connected. I notice that brooks flow into streams, streams flow into rivers, and rivers eventually flow into oceans. These bodies of water are connected because water moves from one place to another."
Model Sentence:
A brook and a river are connected because water flows from smaller bodies of water into larger bodies of water.


Making Connections
• _____ and _____ are connected because _____.
• One connection between _____ and _____ is _____.
• These ideas are related because _____.
Day 2
Skill / Strategy Named
Expanding Simple Sentences
Think-Aloud / Demonstration
"Writers add details to help readers understand their ideas. If I write, 'Water moves,' my reader learns very little. I can expand the sentence by adding where the water moves and how it moves."
Model:
Water moves.
Expanded:
Water moves from streams into rivers and eventually reaches the ocean.


Day 3
Skill / Strategy Named
Combining Related Ideas
Think-Aloud / Demonstration
"Sometimes two short sentences share a similar idea. Writers can combine them into one stronger sentence."
Model:
Streams carry water.
Rivers carry water.
Combined:
Streams and rivers carry water through the water system.
Anchor Chart
Combining Sentences
and
because
so
Day 4
Skill / Strategy Named
Rearranging Sentences for Clarity
Think-Aloud / Demonstration
"Good writers think about the order of their ideas. Readers understand writing better when events and ideas are organized logically."
Model:
Water reaches the ocean.
Streams flow into rivers.
Improved:
Streams flow into rivers before water reaches the ocean.
Anchor Chart
Organizing Ideas
First
Next
Then
Finally
Day 5
"This week we learned how to explain connections, expand sentences, combine ideas, and organize information. Today I will use all of those skills together in my writing."
Model Paragraph

I DO  —  Teacher Modeling  (Explicit Instruction)
Skill / Strategy Named

	Think-Aloud / Demonstration
	 Day 1
Review the Edit step of the writing process.
Think-Aloud:
"Editing helps writers make sure their writing is correct and easy for readers to understand."
Day 2
Model checking for capital letters at the beginning of sentences.
Think-Aloud:
"I can reread each sentence and check that it begins with a capital letter."
Day 3
Model checking for spaces between words.
Think-Aloud:
"Spaces help readers tell where one word ends and another word begins."
Day 4
Model checking for punctuation at the end of sentences.
Think-Aloud:
"I need to make sure every sentence ends with a period, question mark, or exclamation point."
Day 5
Model using the entire Edit Checklist to review an explanatory paragraph.
Think-Aloud:
"If I notice something missing, I can make corrections before publishing."

SECTION 6: DIFFERENTIATION & TRANSCRIPTION SUPPORT
Students Needing Extended Scaffolds
	Provide a copy of the Edit Checklist with visual examples of each editing skill.
Review one editing skill at a time:
• Capital letters
• Spaces between words
• End punctuation
Meet with students in a small group to model how to locate and correct errors in a draft.
Provide sentence examples showing:
Incorrect: water moves through rivers
Correct: Water moves through rivers.
Students may:
• Highlight errors before correcting them
• Verbally explain edits to a teacher or partner
• Participate in shared editing before independently editing their own draft
Sentence Frames:
• I fixed a _____ letter.
• I added a _____.
• I corrected _____.


	Students Approaching Independence
	Provide:
• Edit Checklist
• Peer editing opportunities
• Color-coded editing tools (highlighters, colored pencils)
Encourage students to edit one checklist item at a time.
Checklist:
□ I checked capital letters.
□ I checked spaces.
□ I checked punctuation.
□ I fixed mistakes I found.
Students discuss edits with a partner before making corrections independently.


	Students Who Are Independent
	Challenge students to:
• Explain why edits improve readability.
• Identify additional errors not listed on the checklist.
• Support peers during editing conferences.
• Review sentence fluency while editing.
• Prepare writing for publishing by ensuring all edits are complete. 
	ELL/Multilingual Learners
	Provide:
• Visual examples of correct and incorrect sentences
• Color-coded editing models
• Partner rehearsal before editing
• Teacher modeling and think-alouds
• Bilingual supports when available
Sentence Frames:
• I found a mistake in _____.
• I added a capital letter.
• I added punctuation.
Students may orally explain edits before making corrections in writing.


	Transcription Demands Addressed
	Students focus on editing conventions after ideas have already been developed during planning, drafting, and revising. The Edit Checklist breaks editing into manageable steps so students can focus on one skill at a time. Teacher modeling, oral rehearsal, peer support, color-coded editing tools, and visual examples reduce cognitive load while reinforcing capitalization, spacing, and punctuation conventions. Students are encouraged to reread their writing aloud to identify errors and improve overall readability before publishing.
